verdicts.trueWording: A senator, Plautus Bonosus, remembers the scene as it unfolded before him
verdicts.note: Raw page (brightweavings, 'Justinian Visited and Revisited', by Pierre-Louis Malosse, Universite Paul Valery, first published Anabases 5 (2007) pp.229-235) fetched via curl. Concluding section carries the quotation word for word, immediately after Malosse says it is 'worth citing a passage to provide a sense of Guy Gavriel Kay's style'. Every limb holds: the cited passage is Theodora/Alixana's speech, and it is framed as senator Plautus Bonosus's memory of the scene 'as it unfolded before him'.

verdicts.trueWording: citing a passage to provide a sense of Guy Gavriel Kay's style
verdicts.note: Same raw page. Full sentence: 'By way of conclusion, it is certainly worth citing a passage to provide a sense of Guy Gavriel Kay's style, especially as compared with the narrative supplied by Procopius17.' Both limbs supported - one passage offered as the style sample, and explicitly set against Procopius's narrative.

verdicts.trueWording: the lapidary fashion in which narratival episodes were laid next to each other
verdicts.note: Raw page (brightweavings /jadslight/, 'In Jad's Light', by Andrew Patton, introduced by Kay as art critic Andy Patton and written inside the in-world 'Sarantine Letters' conceit). Quotation verbatim; the sentence continues 'sometimes making neighbours of vastly different places, ranks of persons, or perspectives', supporting the claim's second limb (claim says 'ranks', page says 'ranks of persons').

verdicts.trueWording: attend carefully to the book's construction at both large and small scales
verdicts.note: Same raw page. Verbatim: 'If you will attend carefully to the book's construction at both large and small scales, in both the writing of sentences and the composing of separate episodes, you will see... that Kay is attempting to convince us that writing, like mosaic, is an art.' Both scales - sentence and episode - are supported.

verdicts.trueWording: attaches an even greater sense of distance and further mythic gravitas
verdicts.note: Live host is behind an AWS WAF challenge (HTTP 202, 0 bytes) for both the landing page and the PDF; recovered the thesis PDF via Wayback raw capture (web.archive.org/web/20240915231703id_/.../viewcontent.cgi?article=4917&context=theses, 1.96 MB) and extracted text with pdfminer. Verbatim on the page numbered 322: 'The adoption of a more formal register for this particular episode appeals to the cultural legacy of older tales. It attaches an even greater sense of distance and further mythic gravitas to this section of Kay's tale.' The episode is Diarmuid's seduction of Sharra, cited throughout to ST = The Summer Tree; thesis is Narelle Campbell, University of Wollongong, 2013.

verdicts.trueWording: ambience and literary resonance obscure the ethnic and gender imbalances
verdicts.note: No quote supplied, so graded on substance; the page's own wording is nearly identical. From the same Wayback-recovered PDF, in the paragraph that begins 'the plausibility of newer stories': 'The ambience and the literary resonance in The Fionavar Tapestry, aided by Kay's knowledge and use of mythic and medieval tropes and traditional narrative patterns, obscure the ethnic and gender imbalances present in the episode of Diarmuid's seduction of Sharra.' The claim's 'mythic' modifier is carried by the page's 'mythic and medieval tropes' clause rather than attached to 'ambience' directly.

verdicts.trueWording: When the narrator's voice reveals itself, it adopts the authority of the club-story teller
verdicts.note: Raw page (brightweavings, Matthew Rettino's 2012 McGill honours thesis) fetched via curl. Quotation verbatim, and the surrounding paragraph is squarely about Tigana (Duke Sandre, Alberico, page cite '(12)'). Page adds 'becoming unquestionable'.

verdicts.trueWording: The omniscient narrator, by revealing that many events in history are not known, subverts
verdicts.note: Same raw page. Verbatim: 'The omniscient narrator, by revealing that many events in history are not known, subverts the role of unquestionable historical narration and exposes the ideology underlying the portal-quest fantasy...' The paragraph is the Under Heaven discussion (Wen Zhou, Teng Pass, Kitai, Spring Rain's lost letter), so the Under Heaven limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: I might polish the prose itself, perhaps adding some gloss notes on character
verdicts.note: Raw page (d.lib.rochester.edu Camelot Project, Raymond H. Thompson interview, Mythcon Vancouver, 30 July 1989) fetched via curl; quotation is verbatim. Date, work (the Fionavar trilogy - 'before the characters from our world cross to Fionavar'), and 'opening chapters' ('the first few chapters') all check out. The one limb the page does not carry is the flat 'would': Kay's definite 'would' attaches to paying attention to the first few chapters, while polishing the prose is explicitly hedged as 'I might'. Cure by rewording to 'said he might polish the prose'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the definite 'would polish' - the page says only 'I might polish the prose itself'

verdicts.trueWording: creating a 'secondary world' and investing it with the consistency of reality
verdicts.note: Raw page (brightweavings /worldbuilding/, 'The World-Building of Guy Gavriel Kay' by Holly E. Ordway, dated May 13, 1998) fetched via curl. Verbatim in the second paragraph: 'What I have set out to do in this paper is to explore some of the ways that fantasist Guy Gavriel Kay has gone about creating a “secondary world” and investing it with the consistency of reality.' Note: the page carries author and date but makes no mention of UMass Amherst or of an independent study - that detail sits in the source field, not in the claim sentence, so it does not affect the grade.

verdicts.trueWording: Kay draws on literature, mythology, and history as well as his own imagination
verdicts.note: Same raw page, same paragraph: 'Kay draws on literature, mythology, and history as well as his own imagination to create the worlds of his fantasy novels.' Quotation verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the major events have their genesis in the emphatically freely willed actions performed by the protagonists
verdicts.note: Raw page (brightweavings /webbtigana/, by Janeen Webb, (c) 1991, first published in The Ring Bearer: Journal of the Mythopoeic Literature Society of Australia, Spring 1991, Vol 8 No 2) fetched via curl. Quotation verbatim; the page continues 'performed by the protagonists on the relevant Ember Days', so the protagonists limb is supported and the claim merely omits the Ember Days qualifier.

verdicts.trueWording: central metaphors form an integral artistic system representing formation, loss and restoration
verdicts.note: No quote supplied, so graded on substance. PDF fetched live from elar.urfu.ru (374 KB, 8 pp.) and text extracted with pdfminer; the English abstract on the final page reads: 'It is proved that the central metaphors of the novel (“the lost name”, “distorted memory”, “music”) form an integral artistic system representing the processes of formation, loss and restoration of national identity. The research material is Guy Gavriel Kay's novel “Tigana”.' Byline confirmed: 'M. R. Doshlova - KubSU, Krasnodar (Russia)'. Claim's 'single artistic system' = 'integral artistic system'; 'recovery' = 'restoration'.

verdicts.trueWording: the flavor of Italy is there—in the word structure, the place names, the characters
verdicts.note: Raw page (reactormag.com, 'Altering the Familiar: Tigana by Guy Gavriel Kay', By Joshua Palmatier, in the 'That Was Awesome! Writers on Writing' series) fetched via curl. Quotation verbatim, and the sentence names the characters as well: '...the place names, the characters; in the gestures, the traditions, the everyday force of life moving people forward.'

verdicts.trueWording: not in the use of language, but in the subtle way he skews a familiar setting
verdicts.note: Same raw page, final body paragraph, verbatim: 'Most writers, when speaking of Guy Gavriel Kay's work, talk of his deft and lyrical skill with language... But for me, the true art of Kay's work is not in the use of language, but in the subtle way he skews what is so obviously a familiar setting into something fantastical and mysterious and completely different.' Both limbs hold: the common view is named and set aside, and the art is relocated to the alteration of a familiar setting.
